question: With around 3 million stray dogs and cats1, Greece has one of the most serious stray animal problems in the European Union. This number corresponds to a very high stray-to-inhabitant ratio, although the absence of a single European registration mechanism does not allow for a full comparison across Member States.

There are estimated to be more than 100 million stray animals on the streets of Europe as a whole2, with a number of countries having systematically developed tools for registering, tagging, and preventing abandonment. In Greece, the problem concerns animal welfare, road accidents and – most importantly – the public safety of citizens.

Especially in the area of Pylaia (Thessaloniki)3, there are frequent incidents involving threatening dogs. One even resulted in the death of a 65-year old individual, a case in which the municipality was found liable by the court4. With this in mind, can the Commission say: 1.

Does it intend to promote a common European framework for the registration of dogs and cats in order to reliably assess the situation in each Member State and to enhance the detection of animal abandonment and the accountability of owners?
Will it specifically examine the link between the problem of stray animals and public safety issues, such as attacks on citizens, aggressive packs and road accidents?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) 1. The Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability1 will establish an EUwide traceability system for the identification and registration of dogs and cats. This system will consist of national databases that are interoperable across the Union.

It will be developed in a stepwise manner and will become fully operational within five years from the entry into force of the Regulation. From four years from the entry into force of the Regulation, operators of breeding and selling establishments, shelters and foster homes will be required to ensure that dogs and cats are identified by means of a microchip and registered in a national database.

The same obligation will apply to pet owners from ten years from entry into force in the case of dogs, and from fifteen years from entry into force in the case of cats. These measures are expected to discourage the abandonment of dogs and cats and strengthen accountability in relation to such acts. 2.

The management of stray dog and cat populations, including considerations related to public safety, falls and will continue to fall within the exclusive competence of the Member States, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity and in line with the relevant international standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health.
